topic.subject: social
topic.title: Political parties
topic.scope: functions of parties, party systems, national and state parties, challenges, reforms

misconceptions.statement: Political parties and the government are the same entity.
misconceptions.why: Students often see party leaders acting as ministers and fail to distinguish between the party organization and the state machinery.
misconceptions.fix: A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections, while the government is the body that exercises executive power.

probe.question: If a party loses an election, does the government cease to exist?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the party is the government.

misconceptions.root_belief: different labels refer to the same thing

misconceptions.statement: A multi-party system is always better than a two-party system.
misconceptions.why: Students equate 'more' with 'better' in a democratic context without considering stability.
misconceptions.fix: No system is inherently better; multi-party systems offer more choice but can lead to instability, while two-party systems are more stable.

probe.question: Which system is the most democratic?
probe.wrong_answer: Multi-party system because it has more parties.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Any party that wins a few seats in a state is automatically a state party.
misconceptions.why: Students ignore the specific percentage and seat criteria set by the Election Commission.
misconceptions.fix: A party must secure at least 6% of the total votes in a legislative assembly election and win at least two seats to be recognized as a state party.

probe.question: If a party wins 1 seat in a state, is it a state party?

misconceptions.root_belief: rules are flexible and based on intuition

misconceptions.statement: Dynastic succession is only a problem in monarchies, not democracies.
misconceptions.why: Students associate 'dynasty' solely with historical kings and queens.
misconceptions.fix: Dynastic succession occurs in democracies when top positions are held by members of one family, limiting opportunities for ordinary workers.

probe.question: Can a democracy have a dynasty?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Opposition parties have no role in policy making because only the ruling party makes policies.
misconceptions.why: Students link policy making only with those in power and see opposition as merely criticising.
misconceptions.fix: Parties in opposition voice different views, criticise failures, mobilise opinion and force the government to modify policies; they also put forward alternative policies.

probe.question: Does a party that lost the election have any role in shaping policy?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only the winning party makes policy; the opposition just complains.

misconceptions.root_belief: Only the ruling group influences policy

misconceptions.statement: The party that wins the most seats always forms the government, even without a majority.
misconceptions.fix: A party or alliance needs majority support (272 of 543 in Lok Sabha). If no party has it, parties form a coalition.

probe.question: A party wins 200 of 543 seats and no other party joins it. Can it form the government?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has the most seats.

misconceptions.statement: India has a two-party system because Congress and BJP are the only parties that matter.
misconceptions.why: Media focus on two big national parties hides the many regional parties in coalitions.
misconceptions.fix: India has a multi-party system: many parties compete and several win seats and join alliances; no single party usually wins alone.

probe.question: Which party system does India have?
probe.wrong_answer: A two-party system, with Congress and BJP.

misconceptions.root_belief: Biggest parties represent the entire system

misconceptions.statement: A two-party system means only two parties are allowed to contest elections.
misconceptions.why: Students read the name literally as a legal limit.
misconceptions.fix: In a two-party system, many parties may contest but only two have a real chance of winning, as in the USA and UK.

probe.question: Can a third party contest elections in the USA?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only two parties are allowed by law.

misconceptions.root_belief: Party system is set by law

misconceptions.statement: A party becomes a national party by contesting elections in many states.
misconceptions.why: Students think spread of candidates is enough, ignoring votes or seats.
misconceptions.fix: A party must win at least 6% votes in Lok Sabha or Assembly elections in four states and win at least four Lok Sabha seats, or win 2% seats from at least three states.

probe.question: A party contests in 15 states but wins few votes. Is it a national party?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it contests in many states.

misconceptions.statement: The Election Commission gives state party status to any party that wins 6% of votes anywhere.
misconceptions.why: Students recall '6%' but forget the seat condition and the state in which it is earned.
misconceptions.fix: A state party must secure at least 6% of votes in an Assembly election in that state and also win at least two seats.

probe.question: A party gets 7% votes in a state but wins no seats. Is it a state party?

misconceptions.root_belief: One vote percentage alone decides status

misconceptions.statement: Internal democracy is unnecessary because voters already choose leaders in elections.
misconceptions.why: Students think public elections make a party's own working democratic.
misconceptions.fix: Parties often lack open membership registers, regular organisational elections and independent decisions; leaders hold power, so reforms such as mandatory internal elections are recommended.

probe.question: Why should parties hold internal elections?
probe.wrong_answer: No need, since the public already elects them.

misconceptions.root_belief: Public elections make parties internally democratic

misconceptions.statement: A one-party system is democratic as long as the single party wins elections.
misconceptions.why: Students equate winning elections with democracy.
misconceptions.fix: Democracy needs free choice and competition; in a one-party system, as in China, voters cannot choose among parties, so it is not a good democratic option.

probe.question: Is a country with only one party and regular elections democratic?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because elections are held and the party wins.

misconceptions.root_belief: Elections alone make a system democratic
